title: 170,000 Salvadorans Face Uncertain Future as Trump Targets Their Protected Status
excerpt: Their Temporary Protected Status was set to expire September 9, but DHS has not announced a decision — leaving a community that has lived legally in the US for 25 years in limbo.
body:
• Around 170,000 Salvadoran immigrants are the next target of the Trump administration's effort to end Temporary Protected Status — the humanitarian program that has let them live and work legally in the US since March 2001, after two devastating earthquakes.
  • The protections were scheduled to expire on September 9, but DHS has not announced a decision. "An announcement on El Salvador's TPS will be made at the appropriate time," the department said. "Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection."
  • About 152,000 of the holders are in the US workforce, contributing roughly $5.4 billion to the economy, according to the National TPS Alliance.
  • A federal judge in San Francisco has temporarily blocked the administration from stripping TPS for El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Sudan — about 300,000 people — while broader litigation plays out.

Soledad Miranda is packing boxes for a move she hopes she won't have to make. "I feel defeated," she told CNN en Español. For 25 years, the program known as Temporary Protected Status has allowed Miranda and around 170,000 other Salvadorans to work legally in the United States and shielded them from deportation. Now they are waiting on a single government announcement that could end a quarter-century of legal life in America.

Their protections were scheduled to expire on September 9. Instead of a decision, the Department of Homeland Security issued a holding statement: "An announcement on El Salvador's TPS will be made at the appropriate time. Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection." The USCIS website says work authorization will also be extended — for now.

A program from the 2001 earthquakes

TPS was granted to El Salvador following two devastating earthquakes in 2001 that left hundreds of thousands homeless, displaced more than one-sixth of the country's population and killed thousands. The program, created by Congress in 1990, allows people already in the US to remain and work legally if their home countries are hit by natural disasters, armed conflict or other extraordinary conditions.

Jose Urias built his life on New York's Long Island after arriving three decades ago as a teenager from El Salvador. As a residential developer, he has built 150 homes and apartments over the years, Bloomberg Law reported, and now may be forced to leave the country. In Texas, National TPS Alliance coordinator Jose Palma — who first obtained TPS in 2001 and has renewed his work permits 14 times since — says, "I'm going day by day."

The administration's case

President Donald Trump's administration has moved to end temporary protected status for nationals of various countries as part of a broader immigration crackdown that rights advocates condemn as violating due process. "Temporary Protected Status is exactly that—temporary," DHS spokesman Chandler Rebel said in a statement. "For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent."

"All of us are just holding our breath."

— Abel Nuñez, executive director, Central American Resource Center, Washington

The legal tangle

The law requires the DHS secretary to decide whether to extend or terminate TPS at least 60 days before a designation expires; if no determination is made, the protections automatically extend for six months. For a termination to take effect September 9, the administration would have had to publish a notice in the Federal Register in July. It did not — leaving roughly 170,000 Salvadorans in limbo, a pattern USA Today noted the administration has used before, including with Lebanon's designation earlier this year.

Separately, US District Judge Edward Chen in San Francisco issued a preliminary injunction temporarily protecting about 300,000 people from El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Sudan from having their TPS stripped, halting the administration's effort to end the designations for those four nations.

Political pressure is mounting. In July, 80 Democratic members of Congress urged DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to extend TPS rather than send Salvadorans back to "a country beset by documented state-sponsored human rights abuses." This month, more than 270 faith leaders and organizations issued a similar appeal. Some Salvadorans had hoped the rapport between Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and Trump might pave the way for a reprieve, even as the administration revoked protections for many other nationalities.

What's next

The only certainty is the clock: until DHS makes its announcement, protections and work authorization hold. But Salvadoran TPS holders are reluctant to count on a reprieve — and families are already signing guardianship agreements determining who would care for their children if they are detained or deported. The announcement, whenever it comes, will land on a community that has lived legally in America for a quarter-century.
image_caption: A woman speaks during an interview at her home, where packed boxes are visible. Around 170,000 Salvadoran TPS holders are awaiting a Department of Homeland Security decision on their protections.
nri_angle: Indians are not a major TPS group, but the pattern matters: the administration is systematically dismantling humanitarian protections, and diaspora communities are watching how courts and Congress respond.
author: Diaspora Desk
